sources.excerpt: J-Ram homers for 1,000th RBI, receives ovation, as Guards claim AL Central lead. CLEVELAND -- One of the clearest examples of what José Ramírez means to the Guardians is one the Cleveland faithful can relate to. All you had to do was take one look into the Guardians’ dugout on Friday to see it. Ramírez belted a solo home run in the sixth inning of the Guardians’ 5-3 win over the Athletics at Progressive Field, in the opener of a three-game series. The 34-year-old reached 1,000 career RBIs with that blast, which also was No. 297 on his decorated big league résumé. “We all looked at each other, and everyone's got a smile on their face,” second baseman Travis Bazzana said. “You love to see it. You love to see him break milestones, too, like that, especially to see the crowd stand up like that. “He's an incredible, incredible player. When he has those good nights, everyone loves to watch it.” Ramírez joined Earl Averill (1,084) as the only players in Cleveland franchise history to hit the RBI milestone. The home crowd gave him a loud ovation as he took his position at third base in the top of the seventh, when that achievement was displayed on the left-field videoboard. Ramírez, who turned 34 years old on Thursday, is now just the 12th active player with 1,000 career RBIs, joining Freddie Freeman, Paul Goldschmidt, Nolan Arenado, Manny Machado, Giancarlo Stanton, Andrew McCutchen, Carlos Santana, Bryce Harper, Salvador Perez, Mike Trout and Eugenio Suárez. “I like to use those round numbers,” manager Stephen Vogt said. “[It’s] 10 years of 100 RBIs. When you break it down that way, it's incredible what he has accomplished, and he's not even close to being done, right?” The Guardians improved to 79-75 with their third straight win, which helped them regain first place in the American League Central, because the White Sox (78-76) lost, 11-8, to the Tigers. Ramírez (whose towering blast went a Statcast-projected 401 feet and had a 102.4 mph exit velocity) has continued to stack up milestones in recent seasons. He became the Cleveland franchise leader in games played in April. By the end of his career, he could be the most decorated player in team history. But Ramírez has consistently maintained one top priority, even on a night like Friday. “Thank God for the opportunity to play here for this organization and be able to achieve [1,000 RBIs],” Ramírez said through team interpreter Agustin Rivero. “But most important is that we're able to win today, because you guys know what I really want to do here, which is win.” Ramírez has long driven the Guardians’ winning, during the franchise’s run of sustained success over the past decade-plus. His presence has made it feel like Cleveland always has a shot. But this has been an uncharacteristic campaign for him. Friday’s home run was Ramírez’s first since Aug. 30 and just his 12th this season. He entered the day with an uncharacteristic .683 OPS in 117 games, in an injury-impacted campaign after he missed five weeks following left hamate surgery. Ramírez has dealt with the effects of that procedure since he came off the injured list on July 22. As he noted on Friday, it’s something he has to manage each day. It’s the type of injury that he feels good one day, and not so well the next. “But you have to keep grinding,” Ramírez said. “I want to keep working, treat it and see how it goes. The last couple days I’ve felt better, but we know this type of injury can just vary every day.” The past couple days and Friday, Ramírez reminded us he’s always just one swing away from impacting a game in a big way. He went 2-for-4 with a pair of doubles on Wednesday. Along with the homer on Friday, he hit a game-tying RBI single in the fourth inning. We’re accustomed to seeing Ramírez make this game look easy. There is something to be said for how he’s carried himself in a trying season, on a roster full of young talent. “He's such a great example of how to play the game of baseball, how to work, how to prepare yourself every day,” Vogt said. “He's still a great teammate. He's still helping us win games. Obviously, a night like tonight comes through with two huge hits. “It's been a year for Hosey, but he's starting to ramp it up at the right time.” Even as he manages his hand post-surgery, Ramírez is pushing for his No. 1 goal. “The goal is to get the division and get in the playoffs and keep rolling,” Ramírez said. “I love the energy we have right now.”

Jose Ramirez Becomes 2nd Player in Guardians History with 1,000 Career RBIs. José Ramírez reached another career milestone Friday night, becoming the second player in Cleveland Guardians history to record 1,000 career RBIs. Ramírez reached the mark with a solo home run in the sixth inning of Cleveland's 5-3 win over the Athletics at Progressive Field. The homer came off Oakland reliever Seth Johnson and gave the Guardians' star another notable entry in franchise history. The home run was Ramírez's 297th of his career, putting him three away from reaching 300 for the first time. What better way to knock in your 1000th career RBI than a homer? Ramírez also became the 12th active MLB player to reach 1,000 career RBIs. He joined Hall of Famer Earl Averill as the only players in franchise history to reach the mark with Cleveland. The milestone came during another productive night for Ramírez. He went 2-for-4 with a home run and two RBIs as Cleveland picked up an important win against Oakland. Ramírez has appeared in 117 games this season, making 115 starts. He entered Friday batting .232 with 103 hits, 26 doubles, 12 home runs and 51 RBIs. He has also scored 65 runs and stolen 34 bases in 36 attempts across 444 at-bats. The milestone adds another achievement to a career that has already included multiple All-Star selections and a long run as one of Cleveland's most productive players. Cleveland entered Friday's game in a tight American League Central race and improved to 79-75 with the victory. The Guardians moved one game ahead of the White Sox for first place. With the regular season nearing its end, Ramírez's production will remain important as Cleveland tries to hold onto the division lead. For now, the Guardians can celebrate another significant moment from their longtime third baseman, who is closing in on another major career milestone at the same time.

Jose Ramirez reaches 1,000 career RBIs in Guardians' victory. Before retiring, Jose Ramirez will likely own every Cleveland career batting record that exists. On Friday night, he put his name in rare company. With a solo homer in the sixth inning, Ramirez reached 1,000 RBIs and joined Earl Averill as the only players in club history to reach a milestone that underscores the All-Star third baseman's consistency, power and versatility. "I like to use those round numbers," Guardians manager Stephen Vogt said following his club's 5-3 win over the Athletics. "Ten years of 100 RBIs. When you break it down that way, it's incredible what he has accomplished, and he's not even close to being done. Very few people get to do it and really cool to be here to watch it." Ramirez, who has more extra-base hits (666) than any other major leaguer since 2017, is the 12th active player with 1,000 RBIs. He is just 84 behind Averill, a Hall of Famer who played for Cleveland from 1929 to 1939 and who may be surpassed by Ramirez in every offensive category. In the win, Ramirez posted his 38th career game with a home run and a stolen base, tying Shohei Ohtani for second most among active players, according to ESPN Research. Mike Trout is the current leader with 40. After rounding the bases, Ramirez was serenaded with the familiar "Ho-sey, Ho-sey, Ho-sey, Ho-sey" chant by the sellout crowd at Progressive Field that watched the Guardians rally from a 3-0 deficit to stay atop the American League Central. When Ramirez took his spot in the infield, his image was shown on the giant scoreboard to salute his 1,000-RBIs achievement and he received another rousing ovation. Following the game, Ramirez was typically humble. "It's very important to thank God for that opportunity to play here in this organization and be able to achieve that," he said through interpreter Augie Rivero. "But the most important part is that we're able to win today because you guys know what I really want to do here, which is win." This hasn't been a seamless season for Ramirez, who turned 34 on Thursday. He struggled early before sustaining a left hand fracture while taking a hard swing June 16 against the Detroit Tigers. He had surgery three days later and went on the injured list for just the second time. Ramirez missed 30 games and returned to the lineup without going on a rehab assignment. He has played with some discomfort since, and there have been junctures when he hasn't looked like himself -- understandable given the severity of his injury. He has looked better of late but acknowledged he is not close to 100%. "I keep working on it every day," he said. "I have to keep working on the training room every day because this type of injury is the type -- one day you feel good, the next one you don't feel so well. But you have to keep grinding." That's who he is, and it's who Ramirez has always been. He has set a high standard for himself and teammates. Rookie second baseman Travis Bazzana is inspired by him. "How he shows up every day," Bazzana said when asked what impresses him most. "When he's in between the white lines, he plays hard. He hustles down the line. He goes to make plays and dives and throws it with all his might. "There's nothing that he lets up on, and he's constantly searching for the best version of himself too. He has high standards for himself, but he carries himself up to that day in, day out and plays harder than anyone, which is what it's all about because when you get 13 or 14 years, you can kind of see some effort taper off maybe. You've made a lot of money. You've broke a lot of records and his effort hasn't tapered off."
